messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 18
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: African
  relationship_status: Single
  occupation: Tax Consultant
  trauma_type: Rape
  pcl5: 74

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Shouting: Shouting, Auditory (Door): Doors opening or slamming, Male Presence: Being alone with men
  Threat: Startle to Touch: I react with alarm when someone touches me unexpectedly, Avoid Unfamiliar Places: I avoid going to unfamiliar places because I cannot assess the danger, Threat from Strangers: I feel threatened by strangers approaching me even in ordinary situations
  Memory: Visual Memories: My memories of the frightening event are mostly pictures or images., Emotion Without Image: Sometimes I feel the full emotional intensity of the event without any clear image or memory, Taste Vividness: I can taste what I tasted during the event when the memory returns

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Jamal was only eighteen when the world he had known unraveled in a single, horrifying night. He had just graduated high school and started working as a tax consultant, a job he had taken pride in, believing it would pave the way for his future. It was during a party thrown by a mutual friend that everything changed. Amidst the laughter and music, he had ventured outside for fresh air, feeling overwhelmed by the noise. That was when he was approached by a group of older men, their laughter sinister and their intentions even more so. The next few hours were a blur of terror that left him feeling shattered, not just physically but deep within his soul.

In the weeks following the assault, Jamal found himself retreating into a shell. He could hardly bear to be in his own skin, let alone face the world outside. What haunted him most were the sounds — shouts and laughter that echoed in his mind like a relentless loop. Whenever he heard shouting, even in a distant neighborhood, his heart would race, and he would feel a cold sweat trickle down his back. It was an involuntary reaction, a primal warning that something was wrong, that he was still in danger. He had come to believe that the world outside was fraught with threats lurking in every corner.

Doors became another source of anxiety. The slamming of a door, which had once seemed trivial, now sent him spiraling into panic. He would flinch at the sound, his body tensing as if preparing for an onslaught. Even the simple act of a door being opened could send him into a spiral of dread, reminding him of the moment he felt trapped and powerless. His colleagues at work noticed his growing discomfort, but Jamal brushed it off, laughing nervously when they asked if he was okay. He believed he had to appear strong, to mask the vulnerability that gnawed at him beneath the surface.

The presence of men was also a constant trigger. He would avoid being alone with male colleagues, opting to stay in crowded spaces or to leave the room at any opportunity. What frightened him most was the thought of being trapped again, unable to escape if things turned sour. He was certain that his instincts were right — men were dangerous, and any unfamiliar situation could lead to more harm. This belief isolated him further, as he began to withdraw from social gatherings and even friendly outings. His friends, once a source of comfort, were left confused by his sudden aversion to hang out, and slowly, he found himself increasingly alone.

Jamal’s memories of the assault were vivid but fragmented; they came to him in flashes, like snapshots of a nightmare. He could see the faces of those men, the dark alley, the feeling of being overwhelmed. Sometimes, though, it was not the images that haunted him but the emotions — a wave of terror that would wash over him without warning. He would be sitting at his desk, concentrating on tax forms, when suddenly, he would feel the panic swell in his chest, as if he were reliving the event all over again. The taste of fear lingered in his mouth, reminiscent of the metallic tang of adrenaline that flooded his senses that night.

Despite his best efforts to mask his pain, Jamal's performance at work began to decline. His concentration faltered, and he made careless mistakes on clients’ tax filings. His supervisor pulled him aside for a chat, expressing concern for his well-being. The conversation left him feeling exposed and vulnerable, as if his wounds had been laid bare for someone else to see. In that moment, Jamal realized how deeply the trauma had impacted him, and the weight of his struggles became unbearable.

It was this confrontation with his own limitations that finally led him to seek help. He had hoped that by ignoring his pain, it would eventually fade away. But now, as he sat in the therapist's office, he felt a mix of fear and hope. He was terrified of confronting the memories that haunted him, afraid of what it would mean to relive the night that had fractured his sense of safety. Yet, beneath that fear lay a flicker of hope — the possibility of reclaiming his life, of finding a way to navigate the world without the constant shadow of his trauma. Jamal had come to understand that he could no longer bear this burden alone, and perhaps, just perhaps, healing was within reach.
